title: A bishop is worth the lines it attacks, not the square it stands on. A protected outpost is a knight's measure.

positions.why: On c4 the bishop looks strong: deep in White's half and held by the b5 pawn. But look where its diagonals end: on a2, defended twice, and on f1, empty. From d5 it looks at the f3 knight, with g2 and the king behind it. So 21... Bd5, and 22. a4 now loses to 22... Bxf3 23. gxf3 Qc8, hitting h3 with the kingside wrecked. (21... Bd3 works too: 22. Qxd3 Bh2+ wins the queen, with the d8 rook behind the d6 bishop.) The square was a knight's kind of good; a bishop needs targets.

title: Don't castle, or step the king, into pressure: go where your defenders outnumber their attackers.

positions.why: Before castling, look where the enemy pawns and pieces already point. Black's g- and h-pawns are on their way, the rook stands behind them on h8, the queen and the b7 bishop aim at f3 and g2, and your h3 pawn is the hook: 11. O-O g4 opens lines onto g1 at once. The king is safer in the middle for now, and you have a punch first: 11. d5 shuts the b7 bishop's diagonal and clears c3 for your bishop, to skewer queen and rook: 11... Bxd5 12. Bc3 Qh6 13. Bxh8, or 11... g4 12. Bc3 gxf3 13. Bxf6.

title: Before judging an attack on a king, count the attackers and the defenders that can reach that side, and how many moves each needs.

positions.why: Count who can reach your king, and when. Black: the queen is there, the f8 rook needs two moves (Rf6, Rg6), and the rest follow. You: the queen and bishop on c3 and d3 are shut off by your own pawns on e3 and f2, and the a1 rook is far away. Two attackers arrive before any of them, so a move elsewhere loses: 17. Qc2 Rf6, and the rook comes to g6 with mate to follow. The only defenders in time are the king itself and the f1 rook: 17. Kg2 Rf6 18. Rh1 guards h2, and the king can run by f1 to e1.

title: Always look for the mating lines, yours and theirs: a mate threat forces the reply, so it decides the other moves.

positions.why: Look for the mate first. Your queen on e1 already takes f1, g1 and h1 from White's king; what is missing is one more attacker, not a check. 37... Bb1 threatens 38... Be4+ 39. Kh2 Qh1#, and because that is mate White has no choice of reply: he must give the queen, 38. Qe5 Be4+ 39. Qxe4+ Qxe4+. A check instead, 37... Qd2+ 38. Kf3, forces nothing and lets the king out. A mating line, once seen, tells you which quiet move to play.

title: To promote a passed pawn, secure the promotion square first.

positions.why: The pawn is two steps from d1; ask who controls d1 when it gets there. After 56... d2 57. Ke2 White's king does: the pawn is stopped and soon lost. Rd6 d1=Q 59. Rxd1 Rxd1. The same two moves in the other order win slowly instead of at once.

title: Before you attack or grab something, list the opponent's checks and captures in reply.

positions.why: The f7 pawn is there to take. First list Black's captures after it: the a8 bishop looks down the long diagonal at g2, and behind g2 your h1 rook is boxed in by its own knight. So 13. Bxf7 Bxg2 wins the rook for a bishop (14. Bd5 Bxh1 15. Bxh1 is the best you have). Shut the line and the grabbing can go on in peace: 13. f3 kills that bishop, and then the loose a6 pawn falls to 14. Bxa6.

title: Before a check or a sacrifice, ask what your next move is after the reply. If there is none, don't play it.

positions.why: 7. Qa4+ wins the c4 pawn back; so does the plain 7. Bxc4. Ask of the check what your next move is once it is answered: after 7... Nbd7 8. Bxc4 O-O the queen has nothing to do on a4 and goes home, 9. Qc2; after 7... Bd7 8. Qxc4 she is doing a bishop's job while your own bishop sits on f1. The check gains nothing and gives Black a developing move for free. 7. Bxc4 takes the pawn with the piece that still had to come out, and you castle next.

title: Before a trade, picture the recapture: which piece lands where, and what it does from there.

positions.why: The bishop is hit by the h-pawn, and 12... Bxf3 is the easy way out. Picture the recapture before making the trade: 13. Qxf3 puts White's queen on the f-file beside the c4 bishop, both on f7, and 14. Qxf7# is threatened. 13... Rf8 is forced, castling is gone, and 14. Nf6+ Ke7 leaves your king in the centre. Your capture developed his queen. 12... Be6 retreats to where the bishop guards f7 and challenges both the d5 knight and the c4 bishop.

title: Before a piece lands, ask what can hit it there: knights and pawns first.

positions.why: You want to hit the c3 knight. Before a piece lands, touch every square the enemy knight reaches from where it stands. From c3 one of them is e2, and from e2 it gives check and attacks c1. So 15. Rfc1 loses the exchange to 15... Ne2+ 16. Kf1 Nxc1. Attack the knight from a square it cannot fork: 15. Qc6 hits the knight, both rooks and a6 at once, and 15... Ne2+ 16. Kh1 forks nothing.

title: When two moves both belong to the idea, play first the one that will not be there next move.

positions.why: Everything is ready: the g4 bishop pins the f3 knight, and the queen and the b6 bishop aim at d4. Two moves belong to the idea, ...exd4 and ...Bxf3; which goes first? The one that will not be there next move. The pinned knight waits; the pawn on d4 can move. 14... Bxf3 first lets White skip the recapture with 15. dxe5, hitting your queen, and the target is gone. 14... exd4 first leaves him nothing: 15. cxd4 Bxf3 16. Qxf3 Qxf3 17. gxf3 Bxd4 wins a pawn and wrecks the kingside. And a quiet move, 14... Rad8, lets 15. Be2 break the pin.

title: In the opening, when a pawn can take the centre with tempo (e4, d5), play it before the quiet developing move.

positions.why: The c-pawn attacks d4 and the queen looks at b2. Before defending, ask whether the pawn can simply go forward: 3. d5 steps out of the attack and takes space, b2 is still covered by the bishop on c1, and the queen is left attacking nothing. After 3... d6 4. e4 Nf6 5. Nc3 g6 6. a4 Bg7 7. Nd2 the knight heads for c4 and the queen has to go back. 3. e3 defended instead, shutting in your own bishop, and Black got a fair share of the centre with 3... e6 4. c4 d5.

Nd5 Qd8 7. Qxd4 centralises the queen with a hit on the h8 rook; otherwise d5 follows and Black is cramped. 5. Bd2 guarded b2, which the bishop on c1 guarded already. When the opponent wastes time, ask whether e4 is playable before any quiet move.
